### III-E Research Gaps and Limitations

Despite recent advances, key gaps remain from an AgTD perspective:

• 

Unaddressed Sources of Agentic Technical Debt: Existing studies (e.g., Moralles et al. (2026)) do not adequately address debt arising from autonomous decision-making, dynamic task orchestration, and inter-agent dependencies.

• 

Lack of Unified Modeling for AgTD Propagation: Current research lacks systematic approaches to model how technical debt propagates across agent interactions, coordination workflows, and emergent system behaviors, which serve as key pathways through which AgTD accumulates and amplifies at the system level.

• 

Insufficient Governance for Autonomous Systems: While frameworks such as TRiSM Raza et al. (2026a) provide foundations for trust, risk, and security management, they do not fully address accountability, traceability, and control challenges in agentic ecosystems. These governance gaps can contribute to the accumulation of Agentic Technical Debt (AgTD) by limiting the visibility, monitoring, and remediation of debt arising from autonomous decisions, agent interactions, and evolving system behaviors.

• 

Underexplored Security and Coordination Debt: Technical debt arising from inadequate security controls, coordination mechanisms, and agent interaction protocols remains underexplored in agentic systems. Such debt can increase susceptibility to risks such as adversarial manipulation and coordination failures Rashid et al. (2025), limiting proactive mitigation and system resilience.

• 

Underexplored Sustainability Technical Debt: Although recent studies have extensively discussed trustworthiness, safety, security, and governance in Agentic AI Raza et al. (2025); Raheem and Hossain (2025); Leo et al. (2026); Adabara et al. (2025); Qi et al. (2026), the sustainability implications of AgTD remain largely unexplored. Agentic AI systems are inherently computationally intensive due to continuous reasoning, autonomous planning, persistent memory management, repeated inference, multi-agent communication, and frequent tool orchestration Abou Ali et al. (2026). Design deficiencies and inefficient workflow structures may therefore accumulate as SusTD, leading to excessive energy consumption, increased operational costs, inefficient resource utilization, and a larger carbon footprint throughout the system lifecycle. Despite the growing emphasis on Green AI and sustainable software engineering Cruz et al. (2025); Alloghani (2023), sustainability has received limited attention as a distinct manifestation of AgTD, highlighting an important research gap for future investigation.

### III-F Positioning of This Work

While prior studies provide comprehensive insights into the concepts, architectures, applications, and governance of Agentic AI, they largely overlook its implications for software quality, long-term system sustainability, and software engineering practices. In particular, existing research does not explicitly conceptualize how the autonomous, adaptive, collaborative, and persistent nature of agentic systems gives rise to new forms of technical debt that extend beyond both traditional technical debt and AI Technical Debt (AITD).

This paper addresses this gap by introducing Agentic Technical Debt (AgTD) as a foundational software engineering construct for understanding and managing technical debt in Agentic AI systems. Building upon a previously validated taxonomy of 31 AITDs Tukur et al. (2026), this work presents a theory-informed methodology for systematically transforming established AITDs into their corresponding agentic manifestations through transformation semantics.
